segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Hi there, Martin. How are you going with your Australian studies tutorial paper?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Oh good. I’ve finished it actually.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Lucky you. What did you do it on? I’m still trying to find an interesting topic.

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Well after some consideration I decided to look at the history of banana growing in Australia.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: (surprised) Banana growing!

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Yes, banana growing.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: (sarcastically) Fascinating, I'm sure!

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Well it's not as boring as you'd think. And I wanted to tie it in to the work I've been doing on primary industries and the economy. Anyway I bet there are a few things you didn't know about bananas!

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Such as?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Such as the fact that bananas were among the first plants ever to be domesticated.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Yes, they're an extremely nourishing food.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: I suppose you're going to tell me the whole history of banana growing now aren't you?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Well, it'd be a good practice run for my tutorial next week. I'll do the same for you some time.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: OK. Fire away. So where were these bananas first domesticated?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: According to my research, the Cavendish banana, which is a type of banana and the first type to be cultivated here, actually originated in China but they had a fairly roundabout route before they got to Australia.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: You mean they didn't go straight from China to Australia?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: No, they didn't. It seems that in 1826, bananas were taken from South China to England.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: I suppose they would have made a welcome addition to the English diet.

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Yes, I'm sure. Well apparently there was an English Duke who was particularly fond of bananas and he used to cultivate them in his hothouse, which is where you have to grow them in England, of course, because of the cool climate and they became quite popular in the UK. So he was the one responsible for cultivating the Cavendish banana which was then introduced into Australia.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: I see. And we've been growing them ever since?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Yes.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Are they hard to grow?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Well, yes and no. To grow them in your garden, no, not really. But to grow them commercially you need to know what you’re doing. You see you only get one bunch of bananas per tree and it can take up to three years for a tree to bear fruit if you don’t do anything special to it. But this period is greatly reduced with modern growing methods, particularly in plantations where you have perfect tropical conditions.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Right! So what are you looking at? One year? Two years?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: No, no, around 15 months in good conditions for a tree to produce a bunch of bananas. And once you've got your bunch you cut the bunch and the plant down.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: So how do the trees reproduce then?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Well, bananas are normally grown from suckers which spring up around the parent plant, usually just above the plant. They tend to like to grow uphill  or at least that's the common wisdom.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: So that’s why banana plantations are usually on hillsides, is it?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Yes. They grow best like that.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: That’s interesting!

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: If you plant them in rich soil and give them plenty of water at the beginning of summer, then they should be well advanced by the beginning of winter when growth virtually stops. But in a country like England, they're hard to grow, although you can grow them in a hothouse.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: But in Australia, it's not difficult?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: No, though even here, the growers put plastic bags around the bunches to protect them and keep them warm. If you go up to the banana growing districts, you'll see all these banana trees with plastic bags on them.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: But how do they stop the bananas going bad before they reach the shops?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Well, the banana bunches are picked well before the fruit is ripe. Once you cut the bunch, the bananas stop growing but they do continue to ripen. The interesting thing is that once one banana ripens, it gives off a gas which then helps all the others to ripen so they pretty much all ripen within a few hours of each other.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Amazing! So do we export lots of bananas overseas, to Europe and Asia for instance?

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Well, oddly enough, no. I believe New Zealand takes a small proportion of or 32 the crop but otherwise they're mostly grown for the domestic market, which or 31 is surprising when you think about it because we grow an enormous number of bananas each year.

segments.speaker: FIONA
segments.en: Yes, well thank you for all that information. I'm sure the tutorial paper will go really well you certainly seem to have done your research on the subject.

segments.speaker: MARTIN
segments.en: Let's hope so.
